title: 05. LangGraph: Reducers in LangGraph — Complete Beginner's Guide
summary: Every time a node finishes running, it returns a dictionary of updates. LangGraph needs to decide: how do I apply those updates to the current state?
objectives: How to Write ANY Custom Reducer

sections.title: What is a Reducer?
sections.body:
Every time a **node** finishes running, it returns a dictionary of updates.
LangGraph needs to decide: **how do I apply those updates to the current state?**

That decision is made by a **Reducer**.

```
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
Node returns:       │  {"score": 10}                      │
                    └────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                                     │
                    ┌────────────────▼────────────────────┐
                    │          R E D U C E R              │
                    │                                     │
                    │  old value + new value → result     │
                    └────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                                     │
                    ┌────────────────▼────────────────────┐
State becomes:      │  {"score": 35}  (old=25 + new=10)  │
                    └─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Two ways to define state (with & without reducer)

```python
from typing import Annotated
import operator

class MyState(TypedDict):
    name  : str                            # NO reducer → overwrites every time
    score : Annotated[int, operator.add]   # HAS reducer → adds new value to old
    items : Annotated[list, operator.add]  # HAS reducer → appends new list to old
```

> 🎯 **Rule of thumb:**
> - Plain type  → last write **wins** (overwrites)
> - `Annotated[T, reducer_fn]` → reducer **decides** how to merge

### Reducers covered in this notebook

| # | Reducer | Quick description |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Default (overwrite)** | No reducer — last write wins |
| 2 | **`operator.add` — numbers** | Adds numbers together |
| 3 | **`operator.add` — lists** | Concatenates lists |
| 4 | **`add_messages`** | Smart chat-message merging (LangGraph built-in) |
| 5 | **`keep_max`** | Only keeps the highest value |
| 6 | **`merge_dicts`** | Merges two dicts (new keys win) |
| 7 | **`keep_last_n`** | Rolling window — keep only last N items |
| 8 | **`unique_union`** | De-duplicates a list (set union) |
| 9 | **`conditional`** | Only updates if a condition is true |
| 10 | **LLM chatbot** | `add_messages` in a real LLM chatbot |
| 11 | **LLM research agent** | `merge_dicts` with parallel LLM analysis |
| 12 | **LLM story writer** | Rolling window to keep latest chapters |

sections.title: Setup — Imports & LLM
sections.body:
Run this cell first every time you open the notebook.

```python
# ── Standard library ───────────────────────────────────────────
import operator
from typing import Annotated, TypedDict, List, Optional, Any

# ── LangGraph ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages

# ── LangChain messages ─────────────────────────────────────────
from langchain_core.messages import HumanMessage, AIMessage, SystemMessage

# ── Groq LLM ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
from langchain_groq import ChatGroq

GROQ_API_KEY = "<REDACTED_API_KEY>"
MODEL        = "openai/gpt-oss-20b"
llm = ChatGroq(api_key=GROQ_API_KEY, model=MODEL, temperature=0.3)

print("✅ Setup complete! LLM ready →", MODEL)
```

sections.title: Example 1 — Default Reducer: Overwrite (No Annotation)
sections.body:
**What happens:** When you write a plain type (`str`, `int`, `dict`) with NO reducer,
LangGraph simply **replaces** the old value with the new one.

```
State before node:  {"status": "pending",  "score": 50}
Node returns:       {"status": "complete", "score": 99}
State after node:   {"status": "complete", "score": 99}   ← fully replaced!
```

**When to use:** Single values that should always reflect the latest result —
like a status flag, current temperature, or final answer.

```python
# ── State: plain types, NO reducer ─────────────────────────────
class OverwriteState(TypedDict):
    step  : int     # ← no reducer → always overwritten
    status: str     # ← no reducer → always overwritten
    result: str     # ← no reducer → always overwritten

# ── Three nodes, each overwrites the same keys ─────────────────
def node_a(state: OverwriteState):
    print(f"  node_a: step={state['step']}, writing step=1, status='running'")
    return {"step": 1, "status": "running", "result": "A processed input"}

def node_b(state: OverwriteState):
    print(f"  node_b: step={state['step']}, writing step=2, status='done'")
    return {"step": 2, "status": "done", "result": "B overrode A's result!"}

# ── Build graph: A → B ─────────────────────────────────────────
g = StateGraph(OverwriteState)
g.add_node("A", node_a)
g.add_node("B", node_b)
g.add_edge(START, "A")
g.add_edge("A",   "B")
g.add_edge("B",   END)
app = g.compile()

final = app.invoke({"step": 0, "status": "init", "result": ""})
print()
print("Final state:")
print(f"  step   = {final['step']}     ← last writer (node_b) wins")
print(f"  status = {final['status']}      ← last writer (node_b) wins")
print(f"  result = {final['result']}")
print()
print("✅ Default reducer: each node fully overwrites the previous value.")
```

sections.title: Example 2 — operator.add Reducer: Accumulate Numbers
sections.body:
**What happens:** Instead of overwriting, LangGraph **adds** the new value to the old one.
`operator.add` is Python's `+` operator — for integers it means arithmetic addition.

```
State before:   {"total_cost": 10}
Node returns:   {"total_cost": 5}
State after:    {"total_cost": 15}   ← 10 + 5, NOT replaced with 5!
```

**When to use:** Running totals — API costs, token counts, points earned, distance travelled.

```python
class BudgetState(TypedDict):
    total_tokens: Annotated[int, operator.add]   # ← accumulates
    total_cost  : Annotated[float, operator.add] # ← accumulates
    last_model  : str                            # ← plain overwrite

def call_fast_model(state: BudgetState):
    tokens = 120
    cost   = 0.002
    print(f"  call_fast_model → tokens={tokens}, cost=${cost}")
    return {"total_tokens": tokens, "total_cost": cost, "last_model": "fast"}

def call_smart_model(state: BudgetState):
    tokens = 450
    cost   = 0.018
    print(f"  call_smart_model → tokens={tokens}, cost=${cost}")
    return {"total_tokens": tokens, "total_cost": cost, "last_model": "smart"}

def call_vision_model(state: BudgetState):
    tokens = 200
    cost   = 0.008
    print(f"  call_vision_model → tokens={tokens}, cost=${cost}")
    return {"total_tokens": tokens, "total_cost": cost, "last_model": "vision"}

g = StateGraph(BudgetState)
g.add_node("fast",   call_fast_model)
g.add_node("smart",  call_smart_model)
g.add_node("vision", call_vision_model)
g.add_edge(START,   "fast")
g.add_edge("fast",  "smart")
g.add_edge("smart", "vision")
g.add_edge("vision", END)
app = g.compile()

result = app.invoke({"total_tokens": 0, "total_cost": 0.0, "last_model": ""})
print()
print(f"Total tokens used : {result['total_tokens']}   (120+450+200 = 770)")
print(f"Total cost        : ${result['total_cost']:.3f}  (0.002+0.018+0.008 = $0.028)")
print(f"Last model        : {result['last_model']}  (plain overwrite, only last node wins)")
print()
print("✅ operator.add reducer: every node's value is ADDED to the running total.")
```

sections.title: Example 3 — operator.add Reducer: Concatenate Lists
sections.body:
The same `operator.add` also works on **lists** — it concatenates them
(like `list1 + list2` in Python).

```
State before:  {"errors": ["TypeError on line 5"]}
Node returns:  {"errors": ["KeyError on line 12"]}
State after:   {"errors": ["TypeError on line 5", "KeyError on line 12"]}  ← merged!
```

**When to use:** Collecting results from multiple nodes — log entries, found items,
generated ideas, partial results.

```python
class PipelineState(TypedDict):
    logs   : Annotated[list, operator.add]   # ← list concatenation
    errors : Annotated[list, operator.add]   # ← list concatenation
    stage  : str                             # ← plain overwrite

def stage_load(state: PipelineState):
    print("  [LOAD] reading data...")
    return {"stage": "load", "logs": ["[LOAD] 1000 rows read"], "errors": []}

def stage_clean(state: PipelineState):
    print("  [CLEAN] cleaning data...")
    return {
        "stage" : "clean",
        "logs"  : ["[CLEAN] removed 5 nulls", "[CLEAN] fixed 2 types"],
        "errors": ["[CLEAN] WARNING: 3 outliers detected"],
    }

def stage_transform(state: PipelineState):
    print("  [TRANSFORM] transforming data...")
    return {
        "stage": "transform",
        "logs" : ["[TRANSFORM] normalised 10 columns"],
        "errors": [],
    }

g = StateGraph(PipelineState)
g.add_node("load",      stage_load)
g.add_node("clean",     stage_clean)
g.add_node("transform", stage_transform)
g.add_edge(START,       "load")
g.add_edge("load",      "clean")
g.add_edge("clean",     "transform")
g.add_edge("transform", END)
app = g.compile()

result = app.invoke({"logs": [], "errors": [], "stage": ""})
print()
print(f"Final stage: {result['stage']}  (plain overwrite)")
print(f"All logs ({len(result['logs'])}):")
for log in result["logs"]:
    print(f"  {log}")
print(f"All errors/warnings ({len(result['errors'])}):")
for err in result["errors"]:
    print(f"  {err}")
print()
print("✅ operator.add on lists: every node appends its logs to the growing list.")
```

sections.title: Example 4 — add_messages Reducer: Smart Chat History
sections.body:
`add_messages` is LangGraph's **most important built-in reducer**.  
It is specifically designed for **conversation history** and does two smart things:

1. **Appends** new messages to the existing list (like `operator.add`)
2. **Updates in place** if a message with the same `id` is returned (no duplicates!)

```
State before:   messages = [HumanMessage("Hello")]
Node returns:   messages = [AIMessage("Hi there!")]
State after:    messages = [HumanMessage("Hello"), AIMessage("Hi there!")]

   ← operator.add would do the same here, BUT:

If node returns a message with the SAME id as an existing message,
add_messages REPLACES it instead of duplicating it.
This is critical for streaming tokens correctly.
```

**When to use:** Always use `add_messages` (not `operator.add`) for chat messages.

```python
# ── State using add_messages ────────────────────────────────────
class ConvState(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list, add_messages]   # ← LangGraph built-in
    turn    : int                             # ← plain overwrite

# ── Simulate a 3-turn conversation ─────────────────────────────
def human_turn_1(state: ConvState):
    print(f"  turn {state['turn']}: human says hello")
    return {"messages": [HumanMessage("Hi! My name is Arjun.")], "turn": 1}

def ai_turn_1(state: ConvState):
    print(f"  turn {state['turn']}: AI replies")
    return {"messages": [AIMessage("Hello Arjun! Nice to meet you.")], "turn": 1}

def human_turn_2(state: ConvState):
    print(f"  turn {state['turn']}: human asks question")
    return {"messages": [HumanMessage("What's my name again?")], "turn": 2}

def ai_turn_2(state: ConvState):
    print(f"  turn {state['turn']}: AI answers using history")
    return {"messages": [AIMessage("Your name is Arjun, of course!")], "turn": 2}

g = StateGraph(ConvState)
for name, fn in [("h1",human_turn_1),("a1",ai_turn_1),("h2",human_turn_2),("a2",ai_turn_2)]:
    g.add_node(name, fn)
g.add_edge(START, "h1"); g.add_edge("h1","a1")
g.add_edge("a1",  "h2"); g.add_edge("h2","a2")
g.add_edge("a2",  END)
app = g.compile()

result = app.invoke({"messages": [], "turn": 0})
print()
print(f"Total messages in history: {len(result['messages'])}")
for m in result["messages"]:
    role = "Human" if isinstance(m, HumanMessage) else "AI"
    print(f"  [{role}] {m.content}")
print()
print("✅ add_messages: all 4 messages accumulated, none overwritten or duplicated.")

# ── BONUS: show what happens with duplicate IDs (update in place) ─
print()
print("── Bonus: duplicate-ID update demo ──────────────────────────")
from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage as AIM
msg_v1 = AIM(content="Draft reply...", id="msg-99")
msg_v2 = AIM(content="Final reply!",   id="msg-99")  # same id!

state1 = {"messages": [msg_v1], "turn": 0}
# Manually call the reducer to show the behaviour:
from langgraph.graph.message import add_messages as _am
merged = _am(state1["messages"], [msg_v2])
print(f"Messages after update: {len(merged)} (still 1 — updated in place)")
print(f"Content: '{merged[0].content}'")
print("✅ Same id → updated in place, NOT duplicated. This powers streaming.")
```

sections.title: Example 5 — Custom Reducer: keep_max and keep_min
sections.body:
Sometimes you only care about the **best** or **worst** value across all nodes.

```
Multiple nodes compute a confidence score for their answer.
You want the STATE to always hold the BEST (highest) score found so far.

Node A returns: {"confidence": 0.72}
Node B returns: {"confidence": 0.91}   ← higher!
Node C returns: {"confidence": 0.65}

Final state:    {"confidence": 0.91}   ← keep_max kept the winner
```

**When to use:**
- `keep_max` → best score, highest priority, latest version number
- `keep_min` → lowest error rate, cheapest price, minimum latency

```python
# ── Define custom reducers (just 1-line functions!) ────────────
def keep_max(old, new): return max(old, new) if old is not None else new
def keep_min(old, new): return min(old, new) if old is not None else new

# ── State using custom reducers ─────────────────────────────────
class SearchState(TypedDict):
    best_score : Annotated[float, keep_max]   # ← keep highest confidence
    lowest_cost: Annotated[float, keep_min]   # ← keep cheapest option
    attempts   : Annotated[int,   operator.add]  # ← count all attempts
    winner     : str                             # ← overwrite (last wins)

# ── Multiple search strategies each return their score ─────────
def strategy_fast(state: SearchState):
    score, cost = 0.72, 0.002
    print(f"  fast     → score={score}, cost=${cost}")
    return {"best_score": score, "lowest_cost": cost, "attempts": 1, "winner": "fast"}

def strategy_thorough(state: SearchState):
    score, cost = 0.91, 0.018
    print(f"  thorough → score={score}, cost=${cost}")
    return {"best_score": score, "lowest_cost": cost, "attempts": 1, "winner": "thorough"}

def strategy_cheap(state: SearchState):
    score, cost = 0.65, 0.001
    print(f"  cheap    → score={score}, cost=${cost}")
    return {"best_score": score, "lowest_cost": cost, "attempts": 1, "winner": "cheap"}

g = StateGraph(SearchState)
g.add_node("fast",     strategy_fast)
g.add_node("thorough", strategy_thorough)
g.add_node("cheap",    strategy_cheap)
g.add_edge(START,      "fast")
g.add_edge("fast",     "thorough")
g.add_edge("thorough", "cheap")
g.add_edge("cheap",    END)
app = g.compile()

result = app.invoke({"best_score": 0.0, "lowest_cost": 999.0, "attempts": 0, "winner": ""})
print()
print(f"best_score  = {result['best_score']}  (max of 0.72, 0.91, 0.65 → 0.91 ✓)")
print(f"lowest_cost = ${result['lowest_cost']}  (min of 0.002, 0.018, 0.001 → 0.001 ✓)")
print(f"attempts    = {result['attempts']}       (0+1+1+1 = 3 ✓)")
print(f"winner      = {result['winner']}   (plain overwrite → last node 'cheap' wins)")
print()
print("✅ keep_max and keep_min: only the extreme value survives — all others discarded.")
```

sections.title: Example 6 — Custom Reducer: merge_dicts
sections.body:
**What happens:** Each node adds entries to a shared dictionary.
Instead of one node's dict overwriting another's, they are **merged together**.

```
State before:  {"results": {"temperature": 25}}
Node returns:  {"results": {"humidity": 60}}
State after:   {"results": {"temperature": 25, "humidity": 60}}   ← merged!
```

**When to use:** Multiple nodes each fetch a different piece of data
(weather, stock price, news) and you want all of it in one dict.

```python
# ── Custom reducer: merge two dicts (new values overwrite on key clash) ─
def merge_dicts(old: dict, new: dict) -> dict:
    return {**old, **new}   # Python dict merge — new keys win on conflict

# ── State ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class DashboardState(TypedDict):
    data    : Annotated[dict, merge_dicts]   # ← merged from all nodes
    sources : Annotated[list, operator.add]  # ← accumulated list
    ready   : bool

# ── Simulate 3 different data-fetching nodes ───────────────────
def fetch_weather(state: DashboardState):
    print("  fetch_weather → temperature=28°C, condition=sunny")
    return {
        "data"   : {"temperature": "28°C", "condition": "sunny"},
        "sources": ["weather_api"],
        "ready"  : False,
    }

def fetch_stocks(state: DashboardState):
    print("  fetch_stocks → AAPL=182.5, GOOGL=140.2")
    return {
        "data"   : {"AAPL": 182.5, "GOOGL": 140.2},
        "sources": ["stock_api"],
        "ready"  : False,
    }

def fetch_news(state: DashboardState):
    print("  fetch_news → headline captured")
    return {
        "data"   : {"top_headline": "AI reshapes software engineering"},
        "sources": ["news_api"],
        "ready"  : True,
    }

g = StateGraph(DashboardState)
g.add_node("weather", fetch_weather)
g.add_node("stocks",  fetch_stocks)
g.add_node("news",    fetch_news)
g.add_edge(START,     "weather")
g.add_edge("weather", "stocks")
g.add_edge("stocks",  "news")
g.add_edge("news",    END)
app = g.compile()

result = app.invoke({"data": {}, "sources": [], "ready": False})
print()
print("Merged data dict:")
for k, v in result["data"].items():
    print(f"  {k}: {v}")
print(f"Sources used: {result['sources']}")
print(f"Ready: {result['ready']}")
print()
print("✅ merge_dicts: all three nodes contributed to one unified dict.")
```

sections.title: Example 7 — Custom Reducer: keep_last_n (Rolling Window)
sections.body:
**Problem:** If you append forever, the state grows infinitely → uses too much memory.

**Solution:** A rolling-window reducer that **only keeps the last N items**.
Old items are automatically evicted as new ones arrive.

```
Keep last 3:
  After step 1:  ["event1", "event2"]
  After step 2:  ["event1", "event2", "event3"]
  After step 3:  ["event2", "event3", "event4"]   ← event1 evicted!
  After step 4:  ["event3", "event4", "event5"]   ← event2 evicted!
```

**When to use:** Real-time event streams, chat context window management,
recent-activity feeds.

```python
# ── Factory function: create a keep-last-N reducer ─────────────
def make_window(n: int):
    def _reducer(old: list, new: list) -> list:
        return (old + new)[-n:]   # combine then slice to last n
    return _reducer

# ── State: 3 different window sizes ────────────────────────────
class StreamState(TypedDict):
    last_3_events : Annotated[list, make_window(3)]   # ← window=3
    last_5_events : Annotated[list, make_window(5)]   # ← window=5
    all_events    : Annotated[list, operator.add]     # ← no limit (comparison)
    batch_number  : Annotated[int,  operator.add]

# ── Simulate 4 event batches ────────────────────────────────────
def batch(name, events):
    def _node(state: StreamState):
        print(f"  {name}: emitting {events}")
        return {
            "last_3_events": events,
            "last_5_events": events,
            "all_events"   : events,
            "batch_number" : 1,
        }
    return _node

g = StateGraph(StreamState)
g.add_node("b1", batch("batch-1", ["e1","e2"]))
g.add_node("b2", batch("batch-2", ["e3","e4"]))
g.add_node("b3", batch("batch-3", ["e5","e6"]))
g.add_node("b4", batch("batch-4", ["e7","e8","e9"]))
g.add_edge(START,"b1"); g.add_edge("b1","b2")
g.add_edge("b2","b3");  g.add_edge("b3","b4")
g.add_edge("b4",END)
app = g.compile()

result = app.invoke({"last_3_events":[],"last_5_events":[],"all_events":[],"batch_number":0})
print()
print(f"all_events   ({len(result['all_events'])} items): {result['all_events']}")
print(f"last_5_events ({len(result['last_5_events'])} items): {result['last_5_events']}")
print(f"last_3_events ({len(result['last_3_events'])} items): {result['last_3_events']}")
print()
print("✅ keep_last_n: memory stays bounded regardless of how many events flow through.")
```

sections.title: Example 8 — Custom Reducer: unique_union (De-duplicate)
sections.body:
**Problem:** Multiple nodes extract tags/keywords from different documents.
The same word might appear in many documents — you don't want duplicates.

**Solution:** A reducer that performs a **set union** — keeps only unique values.

```
Node A extracts: ["python", "AI", "machine learning"]
Node B extracts: ["AI", "neural networks", "python"]   ← "python" and "AI" duplicate!
Node C extracts: ["deep learning", "AI"]               ← "AI" again!

Without reducer:  ["python","AI","machine learning","AI","neural networks","python","deep learning","AI"]
With unique_union: ["AI","deep learning","machine learning","neural networks","python"]  ← clean!
```

```python
# ── Reducer: set union ─────────────────────────────────────────
def unique_union(old: list, new: list) -> list:
    return sorted(set(old) | set(new))   # sorted for determinism

# ── State ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class TaggingState(TypedDict):
    tags     : Annotated[list, unique_union]   # ← de-duplicated
    raw_tags : Annotated[list, operator.add]   # ← with duplicates (comparison)
    doc_count: Annotated[int,  operator.add]

# ── Three document analysers each extract overlapping tags ─────
def analyse_tech_blog(state: TaggingState):
    tags = ["python", "AI", "machine learning", "tutorial"]
    print(f"  tech_blog  → {tags}")
    return {"tags": tags, "raw_tags": tags, "doc_count": 1}

def analyse_research_paper(state: TaggingState):
    tags = ["AI", "neural networks", "python", "deep learning"]
    print(f"  research   → {tags}")
    return {"tags": tags, "raw_tags": tags, "doc_count": 1}

def analyse_news_article(state: TaggingState):
    tags = ["deep learning", "AI", "GPT", "tutorial"]
    print(f"  news       → {tags}")
    return {"tags": tags, "raw_tags": tags, "doc_count": 1}

g = StateGraph(TaggingState)
g.add_node("blog",    analyse_tech_blog)
g.add_node("paper",   analyse_research_paper)
g.add_node("news",    analyse_news_article)
g.add_edge(START,     "blog")
g.add_edge("blog",    "paper")
g.add_edge("paper",   "news")
g.add_edge("news",    END)
app = g.compile()

result = app.invoke({"tags": [], "raw_tags": [], "doc_count": 0})
print()
print(f"raw_tags ({len(result['raw_tags'])} with duplicates): {result['raw_tags']}")
print(f"tags     ({len(result['tags'])} unique)            : {result['tags']}")
print(f"Documents processed: {result['doc_count']}")
print()
print("✅ unique_union: 12 raw tags → only 7 unique tags. No duplicates!")
```

sections.title: Example 9 — Custom Reducer: Conditional Update
sections.body:
**What happens:** The state only updates when a condition is met.
If the condition is false, the old value is kept unchanged.

**Real example:** A validation score should only update if the new score
is **higher than a threshold** (say, > 0.8 to be "accepted").

```
Current best: 0.75
Node returns: 0.62  → condition fails (0.62 < 0.75) → KEEP 0.75
Node returns: 0.88  → condition passes               → UPDATE to 0.88
Node returns: 0.71  → condition fails (0.71 < 0.88) → KEEP 0.88
```

```python
# ── Conditional reducer: only accept if new value > old ────────
def keep_if_higher(old, new):
    # Only update if new value is strictly higher than old.
    if old is None: return new
    return new if new > old else old

# ── Also: only accept strings if they are non-empty ────────────
def keep_if_nonempty(old: str, new: str) -> str:
    # Only update string if new value is not empty.
    return new if new.strip() else old

# ── State ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class ValidationState(TypedDict):
    best_score: Annotated[float, keep_if_higher]    # ← conditional
    best_label: Annotated[str,   keep_if_nonempty]  # ← conditional
    attempts  : Annotated[int,   operator.add]

# ── Nodes: each "attempt" might or might not improve the score ─
def attempt(name, score, label):
    def _node(state: ValidationState):
        print(f"  {name}: score={score}, label='{label}'")
        return {"best_score": score, "best_label": label, "attempts": 1}
    return _node

g = StateGraph(ValidationState)
g.add_node("a1", attempt("attempt-1", 0.62, "fair"))
g.add_node("a2", attempt("attempt-2", 0.88, "excellent"))
g.add_node("a3", attempt("attempt-3", 0.71, ""))         # empty label!
g.add_node("a4", attempt("attempt-4", 0.55, "poor"))
g.add_edge(START,"a1"); g.add_edge("a1","a2")
g.add_edge("a2","a3");  g.add_edge("a3","a4")
g.add_edge("a4",END)
app = g.compile()

result = app.invoke({"best_score": 0.0, "best_label": "", "attempts": 0})
print()
print(f"best_score = {result['best_score']}  (max of 0.62, 0.88, 0.71, 0.55 → 0.88 ✓)")
print(f"best_label = '{result['best_label']}'   (empty skipped, 'excellent' kept ✓)")
print(f"attempts   = {result['attempts']}         (all 4 counted)")
print()
print("✅ Conditional reducer: state only updates when new value satisfies the rule.")
```

sections.title: Example 10 — LLM Chatbot Using add_messages
sections.body:
Now let's apply reducers to a **real LLM chatbot**.

The `add_messages` reducer is what makes the chatbot remember the conversation.
Without it, every turn would start from scratch!

```
Turn 1: [Human: "I love cats"] → LLM replies
Turn 2: [Human: "What do I love?"]
         ↑ add_messages kept Turn 1's messages, so LLM can answer "cats"!
```

```python
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver

class ChatBotState(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list, add_messages]   # ← the magic reducer!

def chatbot_node(state: ChatBotState):
    print(f"  [chatbot] total messages in context: {len(state['messages'])}")
    # Pass full message history to LLM
    reply = llm.invoke(state["messages"])
    return {"messages": [reply]}

g = StateGraph(ChatBotState)
g.add_node("chatbot", chatbot_node)
g.add_edge(START, "chatbot")
g.add_edge("chatbot", END)
app = g.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())   # persist per thread_id

cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "chat-reducer-demo"}}

conversation = [
    "Hi! My name is Priya and I'm learning LangGraph.",
    "What framework am I learning?",
    "What's my name?",
]

for user_msg in conversation:
    print(f"
👤 You: {user_msg}")
    result = app.invoke(
        {"messages": [HumanMessage(user_msg)]},
        config=cfg
    )
    print(f"🤖 Bot: {result['messages'][-1].content[:200]}")

print()
print(f"Total messages accumulated: {len(result['messages'])}")
print("✅ add_messages reducer: LLM remembers the whole conversation!")
```

sections.title: Example 11 — LLM Research Agent Using merge_dicts
sections.body:
**Scenario:** A research pipeline where different LLM nodes analyse different
aspects of a topic. Each node adds its findings to a shared `analysis` dict.
The `merge_dicts` reducer combines all findings without any node overwriting another.

```
Node "summariser" → analysis["summary"] = "..."
Node "critic"     → analysis["critique"] = "..."
Node "scorer"     → analysis["score"] = "..."

Final state → analysis has ALL three keys merged together!
```

```python
def merge_dicts(old: dict, new: dict) -> dict:
    return {**old, **new}

class ResearchState(TypedDict):
    topic   : str
    analysis: Annotated[dict, merge_dicts]   # ← all LLM outputs merged here
    steps   : Annotated[list, operator.add]

# ── LLM Node 1: Summarise the topic ─────────────────────────────
def summariser(state: ResearchState):
    print("  [summariser] asking LLM...")
    prompt = [
        SystemMessage("You are a research summariser. Be brief — 2 sentences max."),
        HumanMessage(f"Summarise this topic for a beginner: {state['topic']}")
    ]
    reply = llm.invoke(prompt).content.strip()
    return {"analysis": {"summary": reply}, "steps": ["summarised"]}

# ── LLM Node 2: Find pros & cons ────────────────────────────────
def pros_cons_analyst(state: ResearchState):
    print("  [pros_cons_analyst] asking LLM...")
    prompt = [
        SystemMessage("List exactly 2 pros and 2 cons. Use bullet points. Be concise."),
        HumanMessage(f"Pros and cons of: {state['topic']}")
    ]
    reply = llm.invoke(prompt).content.strip()
    return {"analysis": {"pros_cons": reply}, "steps": ["pros_cons done"]}

# ── LLM Node 3: Give a beginner tip ─────────────────────────────
def tip_giver(state: ResearchState):
    print("  [tip_giver] asking LLM...")
    prompt = [
        SystemMessage("Give ONE practical tip for a beginner. One sentence only."),
        HumanMessage(f"Best beginner tip for learning: {state['topic']}")
    ]
    reply = llm.invoke(prompt).content.strip()
    return {"analysis": {"beginner_tip": reply}, "steps": ["tip added"]}

# ── Build graph: chain the 3 LLM nodes ──────────────────────────
g = StateGraph(ResearchState)
g.add_node("summarise", summariser)
g.add_node("analyse",   pros_cons_analyst)
g.add_node("tip",       tip_giver)
g.add_edge(START,       "summarise")
g.add_edge("summarise", "analyse")
g.add_edge("analyse",   "tip")
g.add_edge("tip",       END)
app = g.compile()

result = app.invoke({
    "topic"   : "LangGraph Reducers",
    "analysis": {},
    "steps"   : [],
})

print()
print("=" * 55)
print(f"📋 Research Report: {result['topic']}")
print("=" * 55)
for section, content in result["analysis"].items():
    print(f"
[{section.upper()}]")
    print(content)
print(f"
Steps completed: {result['steps']}")
print("
✅ merge_dicts: 3 LLM nodes each added their piece to the analysis dict!")
```

sections.title: Example 12 — LLM Story Writer Using Rolling Window Reducer
sections.body:
**Scenario:** An LLM writes a story chapter by chapter.
To save tokens (and cost), the LLM only sees the **last 2 chapters** as context.
Older chapters are automatically evicted by the rolling-window reducer.

```
Chapter 1 written  → context: [ch1]
Chapter 2 written  → context: [ch1, ch2]
Chapter 3 written  → context: [ch2, ch3]   ← ch1 evicted!
Chapter 4 written  → context: [ch3, ch4]   ← ch2 evicted!
```

This keeps the LLM context small but still coherent (it always sees the recent past).

```python
WINDOW = 2   # how many chapters to keep in context

def story_window(old: list, new: list) -> list:
    return (old + new)[-WINDOW:]   # rolling window reducer

class StoryState(TypedDict):
    recent_chapters: Annotated[list, story_window]   # ← rolling window!
    all_chapters   : Annotated[list, operator.add]   # ← full history (comparison)
    chapter_num    : Annotated[int,  operator.add]
    genre          : str

# ── LLM node: write next chapter using recent context ──────────
def write_chapter(state: StoryState):
    chapter_num = state["chapter_num"] + 1
    genre       = state["genre"]

    # Only recent chapters go into the prompt
    context = "\n\n".join(
        f"[Chapter {i+1}]: {ch}" for i, ch in enumerate(state["recent_chapters"])
    ) if state["recent_chapters"] else "This is the beginning of the story."

    prompt = [
        SystemMessage(
            f"You are a {genre} story writer. Write ONLY Chapter {chapter_num}. "
            f"Keep it to 2-3 sentences. Continue naturally from the context."
        ),
        HumanMessage(f"Context (recent chapters):\n{context}\n\nWrite Chapter {chapter_num} now.")
    ]
    chapter_text = llm.invoke(prompt).content.strip()
    print(f"  ✍️  Chapter {chapter_num} written ({len(chapter_text)} chars)")
    print(f"     Context had {len(state['recent_chapters'])} recent chapter(s)")
    return {
        "recent_chapters": [chapter_text],   # reducer keeps only last WINDOW
        "all_chapters"   : [chapter_text],   # reducer accumulates ALL
        "chapter_num"    : 1,
        "genre"          : genre,
    }

# ── Build: 4 chapter-writing nodes ──────────────────────────────
g = StateGraph(StoryState)
for i in range(1, 5):
    g.add_node(f"ch{i}", write_chapter)
g.add_edge(START, "ch1")
for i in range(1, 4):
    g.add_edge(f"ch{i}", f"ch{i+1}")
g.add_edge("ch4", END)
app = g.compile()

result = app.invoke({
    "recent_chapters": [],
    "all_chapters"   : [],
    "chapter_num"    : 0,
    "genre"          : "fantasy adventure",
})

print()
print("=" * 55)
print("📖 Full Story")
print("=" * 55)
for i, ch in enumerate(result["all_chapters"], 1):
    print(f"\n[Chapter {i}]")
    print(ch)
print()
print(f"All chapters    : {len(result['all_chapters'])} (operator.add kept them all)")
print(f"Recent chapters : {len(result['recent_chapters'])} (rolling window = {WINDOW})")
print()
print("✅ Rolling window: LLM only ever sees last 2 chapters — saves tokens, stays coherent!")
```

sections.title: All Reducers at a Glance
sections.body:
```
┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
│ Reducer              │ Syntax                           │ Best for                    │
├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
│ Default (overwrite)  │ key: int                         │ Status, current value       │
│ operator.add (num)   │ Annotated[int, operator.add]     │ Totals, counters            │
│ operator.add (list)  │ Annotated[list, operator.add]    │ Accumulate results/logs     │
│ add_messages         │ Annotated[list, add_messages]    │ Chat history (ALWAYS use!)  │
│ keep_max             │ Annotated[float, keep_max]       │ Best score, highest version │
│ keep_min             │ Annotated[float, keep_min]       │ Lowest cost, min error rate │
│ merge_dicts          │ Annotated[dict, merge_dicts]     │ Combine outputs from nodes  │
│ keep_last_n          │ Annotated[list, make_window(n)]  │ Stream events, context cap  │
│ unique_union         │ Annotated[list, unique_union]    │ Tags, keywords, entities    │
│ conditional          │ Annotated[T, your_fn]            │ Only update if rule passes  │
└──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘
```

sections.title: How to Write ANY Custom Reducer
sections.body:
```python
# A reducer is just a function: (old_value, new_value) → result_value
def my_reducer(old, new):
    # ... your logic here ...
    return result

class MyState(TypedDict):
    my_field: Annotated[SomeType, my_reducer]
```

That's it! Any Python function with `(old, new) → result` signature works.

sections.title: Decision Flowchart
sections.body:
```
Does my field need to accumulate across nodes?
│
├── NO  → Plain type (overwrite): `score: int`
│
└── YES → What kind of accumulation?
          │
          ├── Numbers/lists simply combined → `operator.add`
          ├── Chat messages               → `add_messages`
          ├── Keep best value             → `keep_max` / `keep_min`
          ├── Merge dicts together        → `merge_dicts`
          ├── Bounded window of items     → `make_window(n)`
          ├── No duplicates               → `unique_union`
          └── Only update if condition    → write a custom fn!
```

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.body:
1. **Every state key** either uses a reducer or the default (overwrite)
2. **A reducer is just a Python function** — `(old, new) → result`
3. **`add_messages`** is purpose-built for LLM chat — always use it for messages
4. **`operator.add`** works for both numbers AND lists (Python's `+` operator)
5. **Custom reducers** are 1–3 line functions — extremely easy to write
6. **Reducers run automatically** — nodes just return dicts, LangGraph handles the merging

> 🚀 Reducers are the secret ingredient that makes LangGraph state
> powerful and flexible for any AI pipeline!
